This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
The FAA has paused the installation of the routers that were linked to last week's nationwide
ground stop and turned off any that were already installed.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy says officials still don't fully understand the problem.
The root cause of what happened, we don't have clarity yet.
And I promise all of you that when I know what happened with that router, injecting that
overload into our system, I will most definitely share that with you.
If we were subject to a hack, we will share that with you as well.
But all of my intelligence partners are telling me that wasn't the case.
Technicians linked Friday's disruption to a router that had just been installed in El
Dorado, Arkansas.
The routers that malfunctioned last week are being tested in a lab at the headquarters
of the company that installed them named L3Harris.
Transportation Security Secretary Mark Wayne Mullen is defending using a government plane
to attend the LSU Texas college football game as the air industry recovered from the ground
stop last weekend.
Speaking on CNBC, Mullen says he's required to fly on government planes and personally
paid for the trip.
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has broken his silence after stepping down amid reports
he had an affair with a woman who may have been spying for China.
NPR's John Rooch reports Huang says he would return as CEO if the board asked him to.
In a message on X, Huang said he has seen an outpouring of calls for him to return since
he resigned last week.
Huang has admitted to being unfaithful to his wife, and reports from the New York Times
and others said he had a relationship with a Chinese woman who U.S. intelligence agencies
suspect was recruited by Beijing to spy on him.
An online petition to reinstate Huang has gathered nearly 200,000 names, including thousands
of Nvidia employees.
Huang now says he'd be honored to come back if Nvidia's board decides it's in the best
interests of the company, its shareholders, employees and the country.
John Rooch, NPR News.
Britain says it's imposing sanctions on Israeli companies involved in building settlements
in the occupied West Bank and in blocking aid to Gaza.
NPR's Lauren Freya reports Israel calls the move a hostile act.
Back in September, Britain's Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced a toughening of policy
toward Israel, and now he's given details.
The sanctions target eight Israeli construction companies, along with an activist group Britain
says has blocked aid to Gaza.
They'll be cut off from the British financial system barred from doing business in Britain
and have any British assets frozen.
Miliband says illegal Israeli settlements threatened the two-state solution.
His Israeli counterpart Gideon Saar calls these sanctions a hostile act, targeting private,
law-abiding companies, and he accuses Britain of bias and hostility.
Saar says Israel will consider new ways to strengthen those settlements in response.
Lauren Freya, NPR News, in Ramallah in the Israeli-occupied West Bank.
A.I.
stocks led to widespread losses on Wall Street today.
This is NPR News from Washington.
A new UN report says chemicals and many everyday items that tinker with the body's hormones
are a growing threat to human health and the environment, and science now better understands
the harm they cause.
Endocrine-disrupting chemicals, or EDCs, are found in many plastic items -- personal care
products, pharmaceuticals, toys, household goods, electronics and pesticides.
The new report estimates the health-related costs alone from exposure to these chemicals
exceeds $1.1 trillion annually worldwide.
Does locking up students' cell phones at school lead to better test scores and math and reading?
NPR's Corey Turner reports on a new study that suggests yes.
In the U.S., student test scores began a long slide around 2013, about the same time teens
were getting their hands on smartphones.
So in this new study, researchers from Harvard and Dartmouth looked specifically at schools
that adopted cell phone pouches, where kids kept their phones locked away all day.
And then they compared those students to schools without strict phone bans.
They found students in the pouch schools did get a small boost in achievement, equivalent
to what they might learn with one to two extra weeks of school.
A previous study, though, found a close-to-zero effect on test scores.
So these new findings have researchers hopeful, while also saying there's a lot more research
to be done.
Corey Turner, NPR News.
Retired soccer star David Beckham's company is suing beauty group Cody for at least $41
million.
He judges that sales of his fragrances in gas stations and discount stores breached their
licensing agreement and damaged his luxury brand.
Cody has asked a judge to dismiss the case.
